power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Despite extensive medical, psychological, and social research and substantial healthcare investment, chronic pain remains highly prevalent, and a leading cause of years lived with disability.

While multimodal and interdisciplinary treatments are recommended, progress may be limited by the lack of an integrative theoretical framework that captures the complexity of chronic pain across levels of analysis.

We introduce a complex dynamic systems perspective as a unifying theoretical framework in which chronic pain emerges from interactions among biological, psychological, and social components over time, and we present a methodological toolbox based on the network approach to operationalize this perspective by modeling such interactions.
We conducted the first narrative review of network studies in chronic pain, identifying 54 studies published up to June 30, 2026.

Most studies used cross-sectional network models to examine associations among pain-related variables, comorbidity patterns, and group differences, whereas longitudinal and within-person approaches were rare.

Across studies, findings support the view that chronic pain-related factors form interconnected systems; however, substantial heterogeneity in variable selection and study design limits comparability and generalizability.
Overall, current applications provide an important first step toward modeling the complexity of chronic pain but so far remain limited in capturing temporal dynamics and individual-level processes.
Advancing this field will require theory-driven, multi-level, and longitudinal research that aligns network methods with system-level questions.

In the longer term, this approach holds the promise to support the development of parsimonious models of key mechanisms, informing interventions that target not only symptoms but the dynamic processes that sustain chronic pain.
The ICD-11 classification subsumes 19 different conditions as Chronic Primary Pain (CPP; Nicholas et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The ICD-11 classification subsumes 19 different conditions as Chronic Primary Pain (CPP; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Nicholas et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: CPP represents a highly heterogeneous population encompassing a wide range of pain types, substantial variation in personal functioning, and diverse mechanisms contributing to the development and maintenance of chronic pain [2].
text.formatted: CPP represents a highly heterogeneous population encompassing a wide range of pain types, substantial variation in personal functioning, and diverse mechanisms contributing to the development and maintenance of chronic pain <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Prevalence rates remain persistently high, with more than 30% of people worldwide affected despite biotechnical advances and extensive research and treatment efforts over the past decades [2] [3] [4].
text.formatted: Prevalence rates remain persistently high, with more than 30% of people worldwide affected despite biotechnical advances and extensive research and treatment efforts over the past decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Clinical guidelines recommend personalized, multimodal, interdisciplinary treatment approaches [5] [6] [7], reflecting the multifaceted nature of chronic pain.
text.formatted: Clinical guidelines recommend personalized, multimodal, interdisciplinary treatment approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, reflecting the multifaceted nature of chronic pain.

text.text: While bio-psycho-social models have been instrumental in conceptualizing this complexity [8] [9] [10], their constituent elements are often studied in relative isolation, limiting the analysis of their dynamic interactions at the individual level.
text.formatted: While bio-psycho-social models have been instrumental in conceptualizing this complexity <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, their constituent elements are often studied in relative isolation, limiting the analysis of their dynamic interactions at the individual level.

text.text: To address this challenge, we introduce a complex dynamic systems perspective as a unifying theoretical framework.
Originating from fields such as ecology, physics, and systems biology, this perspective conceptualizes phenomena as arising from interactions among multiple interdependent components over time [11].
text.formatted: Originating from fields such as ecology, physics, and systems biology, this perspective conceptualizes phenomena as arising from interactions among multiple interdependent components over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Applied to chronic pain, it provides a framework for integrating biological, psychological, and social processes into a coherent model of how pain arises and persists within people over time [12].
text.formatted: Applied to chronic pain, it provides a framework for integrating biological, psychological, and social processes into a coherent model of how pain arises and persists within people over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, chronic pain can be understood as emerging from continuous interactions among components across various domains, giving rise to self-organizing patterns, feedback loops, and relatively stable states that shape the persistence and variability of pain.
For example, the biopsychosocial model already recognizes that pain is influenced by various factors [9, 13].
text.formatted: For example, the biopsychosocial model already recognizes that pain is influenced by various factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: The fear-avoidance model introduces feedback loops that connect these components, creating a standardized architecture of an interconnected system [14].
text.formatted: The fear-avoidance model introduces feedback loops that connect these components, creating a standardized architecture of an interconnected system <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: The heterogeneity in phenomenology and the dynamic complexity of chronic pain raise the question of how such systems can be studied empirically.

It implies that the focus is shifted from isolated risk factors to the structure and dynamics of the system as a whole and calls for methodological approaches capable of capturing such interdependencies.
The aforementioned, quantitative disciplines offer many methods for analyzing patterns of emergence and recovery that could, in principle, be applied to enhance our understanding of chronic pain.

One of them is the network approach that has become particularly popular in psychiatry and psychology as a methodological framework to model systems of interacting components by representing variables as nodes and their relationships as edges in the past decade [15, 16].
text.formatted: One of them is the network approach that has become particularly popular in psychiatry and psychology as a methodological framework to model systems of interacting components by representing variables as nodes and their relationships as edges in the past decade <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: In this way, network models provide a basic statistical representation of interconnected components, as indicated by conditional dependencies.
This lends itself well to a systems perspective.
More recently, network models have been extended to incorporate within-person changes over time, offering a dynamic perspective on how these interactions evolve in one individual [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: More recently, network models have been extended to incorporate within-person changes over time, offering a dynamic perspective on how these interactions evolve in one individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: While widely adopted in mental health research [20] [21] [22] [23] [24] [25], this process-based approach has not yet been comprehensively introduced and discussed in chronic pain research [12, 26].
text.formatted: While widely adopted in mental health research <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>, this process-based approach has not yet been comprehensively introduced and discussed in chronic pain research <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26]</ref>.

text.text: This narrative review introduces a complex dynamic systems perspective on chronic pain.
It reviews how network approaches have been used thus far, and discusses what is needed to further develop the study of chronic pain within a dynamical systems framework.
First, we outline the systems perspective as a conceptual foundation for understanding chronic pain.
Second, we provide an overview of the methodological toolbox of network analysis.
Third, we review existing studies applying network approaches to chronic pain.
Finally, we evaluate and discuss these findings to inform future directions in the field of chronic pain research from a dynamical complex systems perspective.
Our ability to effect change within a system depends on understanding its underlying dynamics.

Just as repairing a car or a cardiovascular disease demand insight into the workings of their respective systems, advancing treatments for chronic pain and mental health conditions requires a nuanced understanding of how biological, psychological, and social components self-organize and mutually reinforce one another [27].
text.formatted: Just as repairing a car or a cardiovascular disease demand insight into the workings of their respective systems, advancing treatments for chronic pain and mental health conditions requires a nuanced understanding of how biological, psychological, and social components self-organize and mutually reinforce one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: It is essential to describe these system components and their dynamic interactions in order to design interventions that promote flexibility, meaningful change and resilience [28].
text.formatted: It is essential to describe these system components and their dynamic interactions in order to design interventions that promote flexibility, meaningful change and resilience <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: A system is a set of interrelated or interdependent components that form a unified whole with properties that emerge from their interactions [29].
text.formatted: A system is a set of interrelated or interdependent components that form a unified whole with properties that emerge from their interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: Aligning with bio-psycho-social models of chronic pain [2, 8, 9, 30], a complex dynamic systems perspective draws upon theoretical principles from multiple pain disciplines to describe their mutual interactions [31].
text.formatted: Aligning with bio-psycho-social models of chronic pain <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>, a complex dynamic systems perspective draws upon theoretical principles from multiple pain disciplines to describe their mutual interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Complex systems comprise many interacting components that collectively exhibit behaviors such as emergence, adaptation, and self-organization [32].
text.formatted: Complex systems comprise many interacting components that collectively exhibit behaviors such as emergence, adaptation, and self-organization <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Numerous decentralized and simple interactions collectively generate complex behavior that cannot easily be predicted from the properties of individual parts.
Biological ecosystems, social networks, and neural networks are typical examples of complex systems.

Most complex systems are also dynamic systems, which specify precisely how components evolve and interact over time to show patterns of change, whether they reach a stable equilibrium, oscillate, or display chaotic patterns [11].
text.formatted: Most complex systems are also dynamic systems, which specify precisely how components evolve and interact over time to show patterns of change, whether they reach a stable equilibrium, oscillate, or display chaotic patterns <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: 'Attractor states' refer to an equilibrium around which a system tends to fluctuate and re-stabilize, reflecting either a healthy or disordered state [33].
text.formatted: 'Attractor states' refer to an equilibrium around which a system tends to fluctuate and re-stabilize, reflecting either a healthy or disordered state <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Hysteresis, a hallmark of non-linear dynamic systems, means that a system's state depends not only on its current conditions but also on its history.

Once an external input has pushed the system into a new state, removing that input does not necessarily restore the original state, because selfreinforcing interactions among the system's components stabilize the new state.
Applied to pain, this means that once pain has become chronic, it can persist even when precipitating factors fall below the levels that originally triggered it.
The pain system has, in a sense, "learned" pain, so removing the initial trigger is not sufficient to return to the previous state.

Viewing chronic pain through a complex dynamic systems lens highlights how factors operating at multiple levels -biological, psychological, interpersonal, and societal -interact and collectively give rise to emergent patterns of pain experience and behavior over time [12, 34].
text.formatted: Viewing chronic pain through a complex dynamic systems lens highlights how factors operating at multiple levels -biological, psychological, interpersonal, and societal -interact and collectively give rise to emergent patterns of pain experience and behavior over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34]</ref>.

text.text: Existing evidence indicates that subsystems at bio-psycho-social levels exist that resemble dynamical systems: From a neurobiological perspective, pain memories are formed through neurophysiological and biochemical plastic changes in associative learning mechanisms [35, 36].
text.formatted: Existing evidence indicates that subsystems at bio-psycho-social levels exist that resemble dynamical systems: From a neurobiological perspective, pain memories are formed through neurophysiological and biochemical plastic changes in associative learning mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36]</ref>.

text.text: The pain memory also shapes the perception of pain through expectations [37, 38].
text.formatted: The pain memory also shapes the perception of pain through expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38]</ref>.

text.text: Psychologically, pain is an emotional experience that activates fear and avoidance responses, guiding behavior to prevent harm [2, [39] [40] [41].
text.formatted: Psychologically, pain is an emotional experience that activates fear and avoidance responses, guiding behavior to prevent harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Socially, these behaviors can be reinforced or discouraged by interpersonal interactions and environmental contexts [42] [43] [44].
text.formatted: Socially, these behaviors can be reinforced or discouraged by interpersonal interactions and environmental contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>.

text.text: Over time, avoidance behaviors may interfere with valued daily life activities leading to disability and depressive symptoms, which in turn may amplify pain sensitivity and fear.
Theoretically, this could create feedback loops that maintain the system's organization around a stable, maladaptive attractor state reflecting chronicity [12, 45].
text.formatted: Theoretically, this could create feedback loops that maintain the system's organization around a stable, maladaptive attractor state reflecting chronicity <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45]</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, resilient systems balance stability and flexibility [46, 47].
text.formatted: In contrast, resilient systems balance stability and flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47]</ref>.

text.text: They are stable enough to absorb disturbances and reorganize around their attractor state after perturbations, yet flexible enough to transition and reorganize around a new attractor when conditions change [33, 47].
text.formatted: They are stable enough to absorb disturbances and reorganize around their attractor state after perturbations, yet flexible enough to transition and reorganize around a new attractor when conditions change <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47]</ref>.

text.text: In the context of chronic pain, resilience might involve adaptive neuroplasticity, exploratory approach behavior, and supportive social interactions that enable recovery from pain episodes without becoming trapped in maladaptive cycles.
Change, therefore, can be conceptualized as a transition from one stable state through a period of variability to a new, healthier stable state [48, 49].
text.formatted: Change, therefore, can be conceptualized as a transition from one stable state through a period of variability to a new, healthier stable state <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49]</ref>.

text.text: In this way, a systems perspective advances our conceptual understanding of chronic pain and provides a foundation for identifying targets and pathways for effective intervention and recovery.

Network analysis offers a framework for modeling the interplay among many variables within complex and dynamic systems (for recent reviews see: Contreras et al., 2019; McNally, 2021; Robinaugh et al., 2020; Schemer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Network analysis offers a framework for modeling the interplay among many variables within complex and dynamic systems (for recent reviews see: <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Contreras et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">McNally, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Robinaugh et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Schemer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In this approach, components of the system, like biological markers, psychological symptoms, behaviors, or environmental factors are represented as nodes, and their associations as edges, forming a network structure (for an overview for mental health researchers see: Briganti et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In this approach, components of the system, like biological markers, psychological symptoms, behaviors, or environmental factors are represented as nodes, and their associations as edges, forming a network structure (for an overview for mental health researchers see: <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Briganti et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The earliest and simplest approach to construct a network is to observe and visualize connections between nodes.
For instance, the London Underground map represents stations as nodes and lines as connections, and social networks depict individuals linked by their relationships.
Based on the idea of such descriptive networks, other methods -such as perceived and inferential -were developed to construct networks.

Networks have the advantage that they do not rely on a priori distinctions between dependent and independent variables enabling one to capture conditional dependencies that can be interpreted as bidirectional and self-reinforcing relationships among multiple variables.

While other multivariate statistical methods share these features, what makes the network approach unique is its capacity to quantify local and global network properties, capturing system-level organization beyond the behavior of isolated components. [52, 53].
text.formatted: While other multivariate statistical methods share these features, what makes the network approach unique is its capacity to quantify local and global network properties, capturing system-level organization beyond the behavior of isolated components. <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53]</ref>.

text.text: This systemsbased representation can generate hypotheses about the causal links between multiple variables, which can then be tested and potentially translated into within-person models.
Subsequently, we will introduce the three most common approaches to construct networks: cross-sectional networks, temporal networks, and perceived causal networks.
We close with an overview of common network properties.

To illustrate the approaches, we use a hypothetical running example from chronic pain, in which a sample of patients provides the cross-sectional data and one person from this sample is followed over time and reports their own perceived causal network.
Each figure shows a different subset of the variables in this system.

From a complex dynamic systems perspective, cross-sectional networks represent how the equilibrium states of network components correlate with each other across persons (Ryan & Dablander, 2025; Fig. 1).
text.formatted: From a complex dynamic systems perspective, cross-sectional networks represent how the equilibrium states of network components correlate with each other across persons <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ryan & Dablander, 2025</ref>; Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: They map the statistical associations among variables at a given point in time, most often using cross-sectional data aggregated across individuals.
In these networks, connections reflect conditional co-occurring relationships [15].
text.formatted: In these networks, connections reflect conditional co-occurring relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Typically, connections between variables are represented as conditional associations, for instance, partial correlations if the data are multivariate normal [55].
text.formatted: Typically, connections between variables are represented as conditional associations, for instance, partial correlations if the data are multivariate normal <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, the absence of a connection between two nodes indicates that the corresponding variables are conditionally independent given the other variables in the network [56].

text.text: Cross-sectional networks provide a phenomenological snapshot of system organization, depicting how system components are interrelated and how they cluster within a defined context or population.
For example, network models can be used to illustrate comorbidities [16] and some symptoms may be more closely related to each other, forming distinct clusters or communities within the network [57].

text.text: In the context of chronic pain, in a sample of patients, one cluster might include pain intensity, pain-related worry, and disability, whereas another (affective) cluster might comprise sadness and social withdrawal (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: In the context of chronic pain, in a sample of patients, one cluster might include pain intensity, pain-related worry, and disability, whereas another (affective) cluster might comprise sadness and social withdrawal (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: These clusters may be interconnected through bridge symptoms such as sleep problems, which link otherwise distinct communities [58].
text.formatted: These clusters may be interconnected through bridge symptoms such as sleep problems, which link otherwise distinct communities <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref>.

text.text: By visualizing and quantifying such interrelations, cross-sectional networks can reveal connections, subcommunities, and how nodes are connected to other nodes in comparison to each other indicating their centrality to the network (for tutorials see Epskamp et al., 2018; Epskamp & Fried, 2018; Hevey, 2018).

text.text: Cross-sectional network models have been estimated for various mental disorders, including Major Depression [22, 25], Posttraumatic Stress Disorder [20, 61], Social Anxiety Disorder [62], and Eating Disorders [63].

text.text: However, cross-sectional networks are limited in capturing system dynamics and supporting causal inference.

Because they do not consider temporal precedence and conflate within-and between-person relations, inferences about within-person processes are valid only if the strong assumption of ergodicity is met.
Ergodicity means that the same relations hold within every individual over time as in the group on average.

Temporal networks extend this structural snapshot of how equilibrium states of system components co-occur across individuals by modeling how variables interact and influence one another over time within individuals aligning more closely to a complex, dynamical systems perspective.

For example, we might find that, for one person in this sample, sleep problems are temporally preceded by avoidance and drinking alcohol, and that these in turn reinforce pain intensity and pain-related worry.
This creates a vicious cycle where pain-related worry increases avoidance and drinking alcohol, which in turn exacerbate sleep problems (Fig. 2, Weeks 3-4).
text.formatted: This creates a vicious cycle where pain-related worry increases avoidance and drinking alcohol, which in turn exacerbate sleep problems (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>, Weeks 3-4).

text.text: Rather than relying on cross-sectional data, temporal network models are based on longitudinal or time-series data collected from one or multiple individuals [17, 64, 65].
text.formatted: Rather than relying on cross-sectional data, temporal network models are based on longitudinal or time-series data collected from one or multiple individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65]</ref>.

text.text: This allows researchers to capture temporal dependencies and dynamic feedback processes between components of the complex systems within individuals.

Whereas temporal network models can in principle take many shapes, the currently most commonly estimated model is the lag-1 vector autoregressive (VAR) model, consisting of cross-lagged and autoregressive relations [66] [67] [68].

text.text: In these networks, a directed edge (arrow) from one node to another indicates that variation in the first variable predicts variation in the second at the subsequent time point, controlling for all variables at the previous time point.

These temporal associations do not establish definitive causation [69], but they can be interpreted within the framework of Granger causality, which assumes that causes precede their effects in time [70, 71].

Longitudinal-data networks have been applied to investigate the individual dynamics of Mood and Anxiety [67, 80, 81], Social Anxiety Disorder [82], Eating Disorders [83, 84], Posttraumatic Stress Disorder [85], and Personality Disorders [86].

text.text: By quantifying these dynamic interactions, temporal networks enable the study of system dynamics.
They have the potential to explore how chronic maladaptive patterns of functioning self-organize and stabilize and to identify leverage points for intervention.
However, temporal networks are sensitive to the sampling rate [19, 76], and complex models such as time-varying models require large amounts of data to yield reliable estimates [87, 88].

A central feature of network analysis consistent with systems thinking is that complex patterns of behavior emerge from simple local interactions, as captured in the edges of crosssectional and temporal network models.
These emergent dynamics illustrate how interconnected components collectively shape system-level functioning in ways that cannot be inferred from individual elements in isolation.
They can be described at three levels: the topology of the network, the state of the network in terms of node activation, and the trajectories of system dynamics [56].
text.formatted: They can be described at three levels: the topology of the network, the state of the network in terms of node activation, and the trajectories of system dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref>.

text.text: These levels can dissociate.
Individuals with chronic pain may share a similar network topology yet differ substantially in node activation, which may be the more clinically meaningful variable.
So-called network properties summarize some of these system-level aspects, primarily the topology, at both local and global levels.
Whereas local network properties summarize the position and connectivity of individual nodes within the network, global properties describe the organization of the network as a whole.

Local network properties comprise node predictability (proportion of variance of one node predicted by the other nodes of the network; [100] and centrality measures (identifying and quantifying critical positions within the network; [101].

text.text: In cross-sectional networks, strength centrality reflects the weighted sum of all edges connected to a node.

For example, sleep problems are strongly connected to pain-related worry and sadness, and more weakly connected to pain intensity, disability, and social withdrawal, bridging the pain and affective clusters and making it a central node overall (Fig. 1).

text.text: In the context of chronic pain, networks may help clarify mechanisms underlying the transition from acute to chronic pain, as well as individual differences in treatment response and symptom persistence.

text.text: However, to the best of our knowledge this is the first narrative review of the network approach in chronic pain research.
We conducted a search of multiple academic databases, including PubMed, APA PsycInfo, PSYNDEX, and MEDLINE (last update 30th of June 2026).

The search strategy was informed by the conditions of chronic primary pain defined by the ICD-11 [1], which encompasses fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, chronic primary headache, orofacial pain, visceral pain, and musculoskeletal pain.

text.text: Additionally, the terms "chronic primary pain" and "chronic secondary pain" were included in the search criteria.

These chronic pain-related terms were systematically combined with keywords related to network analysis methodologies, including "network analysis," "Bayesian network analysis," and "idiographic network."
The database searches were followed by a forward and backward citation search to identify additional relevant articles.
Our search initially returned 7,669 articles.
Following deduplication and preliminary screening, 2,793 articles underwent detailed review of title, abstract and partly full text, from which 54 studies were included in this review.

The first study was published in 2017 [115], and the most recent in November, 2025 [116, 117], highlighting that the network approach has only recently been introduced into the field of chronic pain (Table S1).

text.text: The reviewed studies can be grouped according to their objectives.
Cross-sectional networks aimed to describe network structure, compare networks across groups, examine comorbidity patterns, changes across time, and intervention-related changes.

Temporal network models aim to capture how symptoms, cognitions, emotions, and behaviors predict one another over time, within and across individuals, in order to identify the dynamic processes that maintain or alleviate chronic pain.
Studies in this category focused on how variables within pain-related systems are interconnected.
Twenty-four studies analyzed existing datasets to explore the pattern and strength of interactions among pain and other symptoms or factors within a cross-sectional network model.

text.text: Most studies focused on node-level or edge-level differences between groups.

Across studies, group differences were most observed in the strength and configuration of relationships, as well as in the centrality of specific variables, whereas differences in the mere presence or absence of associations were less consistently reported.
Only a small number of studies reported statistical differences in connectivity.
Overall, however, the specific patterns of group differences varied considerably across studies, with no consistent set of relationships or central variables emerging.

Interpretation of these findings is further constrained by heterogeneity in both variable selection and the choice of comparison groups, limiting the extent to which results can be generalized across populations.

This line of research investigated whether the structure of symptom networks changes across different time points or periods within the same group, thereby assessing temporal stability or reorganization of networks.

The predominance of cross-sectional designs limits the ability of the network models used in this literature to capture temporal dynamics and to support causal interpretations of interactions.
This highlights the need for longitudinal, temporally resolved approaches, which are currently reflected in only six studies.
Collectively, these limitations reveal a gap between current empirical practice and the complex, dynamic systems perspective that motivated this research.
Closing this gap will require theory-driven, multi-level studies with intensive longitudinal designs that provide the time-series data needed to recover system dynamics.
Beyond statistical modeling, it will also require building formal dynamical systems models that turn the conceptual framework proposed here into testable theory.
This review introduced complex dynamic systems as a unifying framework for chronic pain and examined the network approach as a method for operationalizing it.

Across the reviewed studies, network models have provided initial evidence that symptoms and related factors form interconnected systems, capturing patterns of comorbidity, group differences, and temporal variations within persons.

In particular, cross-sectional network analyses have offered insights into the overall structure of associations and may reflect longer-term or aggregated relationships that are difficult to capture in short-term within-person designs.

At the same time, the findings highlight a substantial gap between the complex, dynamic systems perspective that motivates the use of network models and current empirical practices, which remain largely cross-sectional and group-based and are therefore limited in their ability to capture temporal dynamics and system-level processes.

In this section, we discuss how different network approaches align, or fail to align, with the system-level questions they are intended to address and argue that progress will depend on integrating multiple methodological approaches.
This provides a basis for evaluating current practices and for identifying directions in which network research on chronic pain needs to evolve.

The existing literature has provided several initial insights: First, across studies, symptoms and related factors consistently appear to form interconnected systems, supporting the idea that chronic pain and comorbid conditions can be conceptualized as networked phenomena rather than isolated variables in line with biopsychosocial and fear-avoidance models [9, 13, 14].

text.text: From a complex dynamic systems perspective, the central questions concern how systems behave, how patterns emerge from interactions, and how systems change over time rather than the functioning of isolated components.
Applied to chronic pain, this perspective raises a set of core questions: What defines a pain system?
How do biological, psychological and social components interact within a pain system in a particular context?
How do these interactions give rise to emergent patterns, such as the transition from acute to chronic pain?
Under what conditions can the system reorganize toward a more resilient and functional state, and what characterizes resilience in the context of recurrent pain and perturbation?

To answer the first question, we propose the following definition: A pain system, in the complex dynamic systems sense [11, 29], consists of (1) a set of biological, psychological, and social components [9, 13], (2) the interactions among them, such as feedback loops and causal pathways, and (3) a function, understood in the cybernetic rather than the intentional sense, as the state or pattern that the organization of these interactions tends to maintain [11].
text.formatted: To answer the first question, we propose the following definition: A pain system, in the complex dynamic systems sense <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29]</ref>, consists of (1) a set of biological, psychological, and social components <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>, (2) the interactions among them, such as feedback loops and causal pathways, and (3) a function, understood in the cybernetic rather than the intentional sense, as the state or pattern that the organization of these interactions tends to maintain <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: In acute pain, this function is protection, that is, detecting threat and motivating behavior that prevents harm.

In chronic pain, the system continues to operate in this protective mode but in a miscalibrated way, for example through persistent threat appraisal, avoidance, and heightened vigilance, which in turn stabilize the pain state [2].
text.formatted: In chronic pain, the system continues to operate in this protective mode but in a miscalibrated way, for example through persistent threat appraisal, avoidance, and heightened vigilance, which in turn stabilize the pain state <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Because of these interactions, the system shows emergent properties such as the pain experience, which cannot be reduced to any single component, and can exhibit self-organization and path-dependent transitions (hysteresis).
A pain system, in the complex dynamic systems sense, is defined not by its constituent parts alone but by the nature of their interactions.

Following von Bertalanffy's systems theory and Engel's biopsychosocial model, a system requires four elements: (1) a set of components (biological, psychological, social factors); (2) interactions between the components (feedback loops, causal pathways); (3) discernible boundaries (what counts as 'the system' versus its environment); and (4) emergent properties (pain experience itself, which cannot be reduced to nociception, cognition, or social context in isolation) [13, 29].

text.text: Pain systems are also adaptive, capable of self-organization, learning, and path-dependent state transitions (hysteresis).
This distinguishes them from linear biomedical models (such as the fear-avoidance model) and positions chronic pain as an emergent attractor state within a multi-level network of interacting factors.
Addressing the other questions requires a shift in the level of analysis.
Chronic pain systems are embedded within individuals, and the processes of interest, interaction, emergence, stabilization, and change unfold over time within persons [26].

text.text: Accordingly, the individual represents the primary level of analysis for answering key system questions [173].

text.text: Studying individuals over time allows for the identification of within-person patterns that may subsequently replicate across individuals, thereby revealing both commonalities and meaningful heterogeneity.
This logic has important implications for the choice and interpretation of network models used to study chronic pain.
Crucially, different network approaches address fundamentally different system questions, yet these distinctions are often blurred in empirical practice.
Cross-sectional networks describe how a selected set of components is statistically related within a specific group under the constraints of a given model [107].
text.formatted: Cross-sectional networks describe how a selected set of components is statistically related within a specific group under the constraints of a given model <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">[107]</ref>.

text.text: Temporal networks, in contrast, are designed to elucidate how interactions between system components unfold and change over time or in response to intervention [17, 56].
text.formatted: Temporal networks, in contrast, are designed to elucidate how interactions between system components unfold and change over time or in response to intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56]</ref>.

text.text: Because clinical research and practice are ultimately concerned with how systems change, these temporal approaches are most directly aligned with system-level questions of intervention, resilience, and recovery.
Starting at the individual level and building evidence through replication may ultimately allow for generalization and the identification of meaningful subgroups [173].
text.formatted: Starting at the individual level and building evidence through replication may ultimately allow for generalization and the identification of meaningful subgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">[173]</ref>.

text.text: A central methodological challenge in longitudinal network research concerns the appropriate time scale of measurement.
System components may operate on different temporal rhythms, and mismatches between item reference period, assessment frequency and process dynamics can obscure meaningful relationships [19, 76].

text.text: Hybrid multi-time ecological momentary assessments (EMA), combining fixed, random, and event-contingent prompts in the same protocol might be considered to capture this intraindividual variability.
Another related challenge is the large amount of data required for reliable estimates [87].

Perceived causal networks can complement temporal models by representing causal relations across different time scales while avoiding power requests [172, 174].

text.text: They can capture how patients and therapists understand chronic pain at the individual-level.
In addition, these networks are independent of a particular assessment frequency, enabling reflection on short-and long-term connections [92, 93, 172].
text.formatted: In addition, these networks are independent of a particular assessment frequency, enabling reflection on short-and long-term connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">[92,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">93,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">172]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, they can inform case conceptualization by representing beliefs about causal relationships [93, 174].
text.formatted: Thus, they can inform case conceptualization by representing beliefs about causal relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">[93,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">174]</ref>.

text.text: Future work should also move beyond a narrow focus on traditional centrality metrics toward the development and validation of network properties that better capture system-level dynamics.

Of particular clinical relevance is the potential to detect early warning signals, such as rising variance and increasing temporal autocorrelation in symptom dynamics, that may precede critical transitions from acute to chronic disabling pain, offering a window for timely intervention before the system settles into a maladaptive stable state [175] [176] [177].

text.text: Sufficient intensive longitudinal data that can be assessed using continuous data sources other than selfreport such as accelerometer data, heart rate variability are a precondition to estimating early warning signals of critical transitions.
However, empirical support for early warning signals based on critical slowing down in clinical psychology remains limited [33].
text.formatted: However, empirical support for early warning signals based on critical slowing down in clinical psychology remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Whether these signals occur depends strongly on the specifics of the system, contrary to their reputation as generic indicators, and they are highly sensitive to noise, which may limit their practical utility [178].
text.formatted: Whether these signals occur depends strongly on the specifics of the system, contrary to their reputation as generic indicators, and they are highly sensitive to noise, which may limit their practical utility <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">[178]</ref>.

text.text: From a measurement perspective, reliance on self-report should not be viewed as a weakness per se as stated by many of the reviewed studies.
Instead, self-report remains essential for assessing subjective experiences such as pain, emotions, and cognitions at the psychological level of the system.

However, integrating complementary data sources, such as behavioral, physiological, and social measures [157, 179, 180], can help capture additional system layers and intensive longitudinal data with less measurement burden [147, 166].
text.formatted: However, integrating complementary data sources, such as behavioral, physiological, and social measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">[157,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">179,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">180]</ref>, can help capture additional system layers and intensive longitudinal data with less measurement burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">[147,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b165">166]</ref>.

text.text: Wearables integrated into studies with intensive longitudinal data collection may provide valuable information that is difficult to obtain through self-reporting, such as motion and exploratory behavior [181].
text.formatted: Wearables integrated into studies with intensive longitudinal data collection may provide valuable information that is difficult to obtain through self-reporting, such as motion and exploratory behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b180">[181]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, although network analysis provides a powerful framework for modeling multivariate systems, it is not the only approach consistent with system thinking.

Methods such as Directed Acyclic Graphs, multilevel Hidden Markov Models, Equilibrium Causal Models or Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling may offer complementary insights, particularly for theory building [54, 73, [182] [183] [184].
text.formatted: Methods such as Directed Acyclic Graphs, multilevel Hidden Markov Models, Equilibrium Causal Models or Dynamic Structural Equation Modeling may offer complementary insights, particularly for theory building <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">[182]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b182">[183]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">[184]</ref>.

text.text: Across methods, a shared challenge remains the reliance on linear assumptions, which may inadequately capture non-linear or chaotic system behavior.
Addressing this limitation will be critical for advancing explanatory and clinically meaningful models of chronic pain.
In addition, qualitative measures are needed to provide meaning and context (De Smet et al., 2025).

For instance, in chronic pain research, a network topic modelling approach was employed to examine well-being practices among adults experiencing chronic pain (Cintron et al., 2025), while in psychotherapy research, Large Language Models have been utilised to generate personalised networks based on therapy sessions (Ong et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For instance, in chronic pain research, a network topic modelling approach was employed to examine well-being practices among adults experiencing chronic pain (Cintron et al., 2025), while in psychotherapy research, Large Language Models have been utilised to generate personalised networks based on therapy sessions <ref type="bibr">(Ong et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, measurement strategies should be matched to the system level under investigation rather than ranked by perceived objectivity.

Viewing chronic pain as a complex and dynamic system offers a powerful conceptual framework for integrating biological, psychological, and social processes and for understanding how persistent pain emerges, stabilizes, and changes over time.
Network analysis holds considerable promise as a methodological approach to operationalize this perspective by modeling multivariate interactions and system-level organization.
This review shows that current applications have begun to capture aspects of this complexity but remain limited in representing dynamic, individual-level processes.
Closing this gap will require theory-driven, multi-level, and longitudinal research designs that align network methods more explicitly with the system-level questions they are meant to address.

Starting from individuallevel models and accumulating evidence across persons and studies may reveal recurring system structures and clinically meaningful subgroups [185, 186], and ultimately support parsimonious, empirically grounded models of the key mechanisms and interactions that explain the emergence and maintenance of chronic pain [27].
text.formatted: Starting from individuallevel models and accumulating evidence across persons and studies may reveal recurring system structures and clinically meaningful subgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">[185,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">186]</ref>, and ultimately support parsimonious, empirically grounded models of the key mechanisms and interactions that explain the emergence and maintenance of chronic pain <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Such models could inform interventions that target not only symptoms but the dynamic processes that sustain them, supporting more precise and effective treatment.
